title: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
summary: Why o1-style models spend 900 tokens on 2 + 3, why RL lengthens traces, and how preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO budgets, early exit, effort settings and skipping thinking cut the waste.
outcomes: Explain overthinking and compute outcome and process efficiency for a reasoning trace
Build short-vs-long preference pairs and explain why one reflection round is kept
Explain how loss normalization and negative advantages lengthen responses during RL, and diagnose it
Compute Kimi k1.5 and per-prompt length rewards and their effect on group advantages
Explain how LCPO teaches a model to follow a token budget and why its Max reward is multiplicative
Detect underthinking and apply training-free early exit with a confidence threshold
Choose between budget forcing, effort settings and output caps, and predict their cost and failure modes
Decide when to skip thinking and compare methods on an accuracy-versus-tokens Pareto frontier

blocks.md:
Reasoning models such as OpenAI o1, QwQ and DeepSeek-R1 are trained (often with RL on verifiable rewards, as in GRPO) to write a long **chain of thought** (CoT) before the final answer. Longer chains help on hard problems: this is the sequential form of test-time compute scaling you met in the prerequisite course.

The catch is that length is not chosen per problem. Chen et al. (Tencent AI Lab, 2024) asked QwQ-32B-Preview, a 32-billion-parameter reasoning model from Alibaba's Qwen team, 'what is the answer of 2 plus 3?'. It produced 901 tokens containing 13 separate solutions. Across models, o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional LLMs on this question.

They call this **overthinking**: spending compute on problems that are simple, or whose answer is already settled, with little or no benefit. To study it they split each response into **solutions**, where a solution is any part of the output that states an answer explicitly. Llama-3.3-70B did the splitting.

scenes.caption: The response contains 13 solutions, each ending in an explicit answer. Every single one says 5. Total length: 901 tokens.

Solution 1 already gives the correct answer after 39 tokens. Everything after it cannot raise accuracy: outcome efficiency, the share of tokens spent up to the first correct answer, is 39 / 901 = 4.3%.
GPT-4o clustered the 13 solutions into 7 reasoning strategies (state the fact, split into steps, count objects, subtract back, algebra, other number systems, modular arithmetic).

Only the first solution of each strategy adds diversity: S1, S2, S3, S7, S8, S9, S12, totalling 323 tokens. Process efficiency, the share of tokens in solutions that bring a new strategy, is 323 / 901 = 35.8%.

blocks.prompt: Chen et al. compared easy and hard problems inside MATH500, a set of 500 competition math problems, each tagged with a difficulty level from 1 (easiest) to 5. Do o1-like models write more solution rounds on easy levels (1 to 2) or on hard levels (4 to 5)?
blocks.reveal: **More rounds on the easy levels.** QwQ-32B-Preview averages 3.7 rounds on levels 1 to 2 vs 3.0 on levels 4 to 5; DeepSeek-R1 averages 4.6 vs 3.9. Total tokens still grow with difficulty, but on easy problems a larger share of the tokens is re-solving and re-checking. The same holds across datasets: QwQ averages 3.5 solutions on ASDIV, an easier set of elementary school math word problems, and 3.2 on MATH500.

blocks.md:
Two more findings make the waste concrete. In more than 92% of correctly answered cases, the **first** solution is already correct. And the first solution is usually less than 60% of the tokens: on ASDIV, QwQ's first round averages 287 tokens, only 38.7% of the response.

Later solutions are also repetitive. The share of solutions that introduce a new strategy drops as the index grows; solution 2 is often the same method run again as a double check.

blocks.title: Conventional vs o1-like models (Chen et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: ASDIV (elementary word problems), mean output tokens. Accuracy is 95.6, 96.3, 96.9 and 97.1%: nearly identical, yet the reasoning models use 4.5x and 5.1x the tokens of Llama.
MATH500 (competition math), mean output tokens. Here the long traces buy real accuracy: 75.4 and 86.8% for the conventional models vs 93.0 and 96.4%.
MATH500 outcome efficiency in %. For one-solution models it equals accuracy. The reasoning models score 52.3 and 51.0%: roughly half their tokens come after the first correct answer.

blocks.md: Overthinking does not mean long reasoning is useless. On MATH500 and AIME (the American Invitational Mathematics Examination, a hard high-school contest with 30 problems a year) the long traces are exactly what lifts QwQ and R1 above conventional models. The problem is **allocation**: the same habit of re-solving is applied to 2 + 3 and to an olympiad problem.
Efficient reasoning asks a different question from test-time scaling. Not 'does more thinking help?' but 'how few thinking tokens reach the same accuracy on this particular problem?'

blocks.question: A reasoning model's response has 5 solutions; the first correct answer appears in solution 1 (60 tokens) and the response is 600 tokens. A colleague says 'truncate every response after solution 1 and nothing is lost'. What does Chen et al.'s data say?
options: Correct: later solutions never change the answer, so truncation is free
Mostly right for easy sets, but on hard sets later rounds sometimes fix a wrong first answer, and the authors keep one reflection round for that reason
Wrong: later solutions are where most correct answers first appear
Wrong: the first solution is usually the longest, so truncating saves little
blocks.explain: Over 92% of correct responses are already correct at solution 1, which is why the waste is large. But not 100%: keeping only the first correct solution (FCS) lowered MATH500 accuracy, so their best recipe keeps one extra reflection round (lesson 2).

blocks.question: Why do Chen et al. measure outcome efficiency instead of just counting tokens?
options: Token counts cannot be compared across tokenizers
Outcome efficiency rewards models for being short even when they are wrong
It separates tokens that led to the first correct answer from tokens spent after it, so a long but necessary trace is not penalized
It is the metric the models were trained on
blocks.explain: A 3,000-token AIME solution that is correct only at the end has efficiency near 1. A 900-token answer to 2 + 3 that was right after 39 tokens scores 4.3%. Raw length cannot tell these apart.

lessons.title: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away

blocks.md: To fix overthinking you first need numbers for it. Chen et al. define two efficiency metrics over a test set of $N$ problems. Let $T_i$ be the tokens in response $i$ and $\sigma_i = 1$ if any solution in it is correct.

blocks.tex: \xi_O = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \sigma_i \,\frac{\hat T_i}{T_i}, \qquad \hat T_i = \text{tokens up to the first correct answer}
blocks.caption: Outcome efficiency, $\xi_O$: for each response, the tokens up to the first correct answer, $\hat T_i$, divided by all its tokens, $T_i$, then averaged over the $N$ problems. A wrong response has $\sigma_i = 0$, so it contributes 0.

Process efficiency, $\xi_P$: $D_i$ adds up the lengths of solutions whose strategy is new to that response (flag tau is 1; the superscript m numbers the solution, not a power), divided by all tokens $T_i$, averaged over problems. Correctness is ignored on purpose.

blocks.md: A tiny worked example. Three problems: response A is 600 tokens and first correct at 120; response B is 500 tokens and first correct at 400; response C is 900 tokens and wrong. Then $\xi_O = (120/600 + 400/500 + 0)/3 = (0.2 + 0.8 + 0)/3 = 0.333$. A conventional model that answers once has $\hat T_i = T_i$, so its $\xi_O$ is simply its accuracy and its $\xi_P$ is 1.

blocks.code:
def efficiency(responses):
    """responses: list of lists of solutions (tokens, correct, new_strategy)."""
    xi_o = xi_p = 0.0
    for sols in responses:
        total = sum(t for t, _, _ in sols)
        upto, first_ok = 0, None
        for t, ok, _ in sols:
            upto += t
            if ok:
                first_ok = upto
                break
        if first_ok is not None:          # sigma_i = 1
            xi_o += first_ok / total
        xi_p += sum(t for t, _, new in sols if new) / total
    n = len(responses)
    return xi_o / n, xi_p / n

# QwQ on "2 + 3": 13 solutions, all correct. The paper gives lengths for the
# 7 new-strategy solutions (S1 S2 S3 S7 S8 S9 S12); the other 6 share the
# remaining 578 tokens, split evenly here (it does not change either metric).
lens = [39, 109, 39, 96, 96, 96, 29, 29, 19, 97, 96, 59, 97]
new = [1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
r = [(t, True, bool(f)) for t, f in zip(lens, new)]
print("tokens:", sum(lens))
xo, xp = efficiency([r])
print(f"outcome {xo:.1%}  process {xp:.1%}")
blocks.caption: Runs as shown and prints: tokens: 901, then outcome 4.3%  process 35.8%. The paper gives lengths only for the seven new-strategy solutions (39 + 109 + 39 + 29 + 29 + 19 + 59 = 323); the six repeats share the other 578 tokens, split evenly here, which changes neither metric.

blocks.prompt: Sampling QwQ 10 times per training question, Chen et al. compared the shortest correct sample with the greedy one (decoded by always taking the most likely next token). Which is more efficient, and is the shortest one already free of overthinking?
blocks.reveal: The shortest sample is better on both metrics (outcome 69.8% vs 55.6%, process 80.3% vs 72.6%), with 2.5 instead of 3.1 solutions. But it still contains 2.5 solutions on average, so it still overthinks. That is why they go further and **edit** samples, not just pick short ones.

blocks.md:
The fix is **preference optimization**. Recall that **supervised fine-tuning** (SFT) trains a model to imitate one given response, token by token. **Direct preference optimization** (DPO), from Rafailov et al. (2023), trains on pairs instead: a prompt, a chosen (positive) response and a rejected (negative) one. It starts from the RLHF goal, maximize a reward while staying close to a frozen reference model. Let $\pi$ be the trained model's probability of a response, $\pi_{ref}$ the reference model's, and $\beta$ how tightly it is held close. The best policy for that goal implies reward $= \beta \log(\pi / \pi_{ref})$ plus a term that cancels when two responses are compared, so no separate reward model is needed: the loss pushes the chosen response's log ratio above the rejected one's.

**SimPO** (Simple Preference Optimization, Meng et al., 2024) drops the reference model and scores a response by its average per-token log probability, requiring the chosen one to win by a fixed margin. Here the chosen trace is short and the rejected one long, so the model learns what to move away from.

blocks.caption: SimPO loss for one pair: $y_w$ is the chosen (short) trace, $y_l$ the rejected (long) one, $|y|$ a length in tokens, $\beta$ a scale and $\gamma$ the target margin. Each trace is scored by its average token log probability. Optional: dpo-variants (lesson 6), not a prerequisite, derives it.

blocks.prompt: The chosen trace is about 1,300 tokens, the rejected one about 2,300, and both average -0.5 nats per token, so the model does not yet prefer either per token. With beta = 2.5 and gamma = 1, what is the SimPO loss, and what would it be with summed instead of averaged log probabilities?
blocks.reveal:
**Averaged:** both scores are $2.5 \times (-0.5) = -1.25$, the logit is $0 - 1 = -1$ and the loss is $\log(1 + e) = 1.31$, so there is a real gradient toward the short trace.

**Summed:** the chosen trace scores $-650$ and the rejected $-1{,}150$ nats. The rejected trace looks 500 nats worse purely because it is longer, the logit is huge and the loss is about 0. The pair would teach nothing. Averaging makes the model earn the preference per token, which is what a short-versus-long pair needs.

blocks.title: Self-training pipeline for shorter traces (Chen et al.)

scenes.caption: Self-training: the model generates its own data. Each training question is sampled 10 times at temperature 1.0.
Wrong samples are discarded. Among correct samples, length still varies a lot: the shortest averages 1,051 tokens, the longest 2,259.
Positive example: cut a sample after its first correct solution plus one more correct solution (FCS + Reflection), keeping the shortest such cut among the 10.
Negative example: the longest sampled response. The authors found it gave a clearer contrast than the greedy response.

A preference-optimization step (DPO-style: raise the chosen trace's likelihood relative to the rejected one; the SimPO variant worked best) pushes toward the short trace. The trained model replaces the original.

blocks.md:
Three ways to build a streamlined positive example from a sample:

- **FCS** (first-correct solutions): keep everything up to the first correct solution.
- **FCS + Reflection**: also keep the second correct solution, so the model keeps its habit of checking once.
- **GDS** (greedily diverse solutions): keep later solutions only while they use a new strategy.

blocks.title: MATH500 mean tokens after each recipe (Chen et al., Table 4)

scenes.caption: Baseline QwQ-32B-Preview: 2,407.9 tokens at 93.0% accuracy.
Training on whole shortest samples: SFT cuts only 2.0% (93.2% acc.); DPO reaches 1,929.5 (94.0%); SimPO 1,871.8, a 22.3% cut (92.4%).
Streamlined positives cut much deeper. First-correct-solution only: 1,016 tokens (57.8% cut) but accuracy drops to 91.0%.
Keeping one reflection round: 1,330.7 tokens (44.7% cut) at 92.8%, the chosen default. Greedily diverse solutions: 1,286.1 at 91.8%.

blocks.md: The chosen recipe transfers: with SimPO on FCS + Reflection, tokens drop 48.6% on ASDIV and 46.1% on GSM8K (grade school math word problems), with accuracy 96.9 to 96.8 and 94.8 to 96.0, and on the hard sets GPQA (graduate-level multiple-choice science questions written by experts) and AIME24 (the 2024 AIME) tokens drop 35.4% and 45.6% while accuracy moves 59.6 to 59.1 and 46.7 to 43.3. AIME24 has only 30 problems, so 46.7 to 43.3 is a single problem.

Kimi k1.5, Moonshot AI's 2025 reasoning model, used the same idea at scale under the name **long2short**: shortest rejection sampling (sample $n = 8$ times, fine-tune on the shortest correct response), DPO with the shortest correct answer as positive and longer responses as negatives (longer wrong answers, and correct answers 1.5 times longer than the positive), and plain model merging that averages the weights of a long-CoT and a short-CoT model.

Plain SFT on short samples barely helped here (a 2.0% cut on MATH500). Imitating short traces is weaker than contrasting short against long, because the model never sees what it should move away from.
Cutting after the first correct answer is the most aggressive compression, and it costs accuracy on hard problems. The useful target is 'one solve plus one check', not 'one solve'.

blocks.question: A team builds DPO pairs from a reasoning model's samples. Which pairing best matches what Chen et al. found effective?
options: Chosen: greedy response. Rejected: a random wrong response
Chosen: the longest correct response. Rejected: the shortest one
Chosen: a correct response trimmed to its first correct solution plus one reflection. Rejected: the longest sampled response
Chosen: a response from a non-reasoning model. Rejected: any reasoning-model response
blocks.explain: The positive is a streamlined trace from the model itself, so it stays in-distribution; the negative is the longest sample, which gave a clearer contrast than the greedy response.

blocks.question: Compute: a test set has two problems. Response 1 is 400 tokens, first correct at 100. Response 2 is 800 tokens, first correct at 800. What is the outcome efficiency?
blocks.explain: $(100/400 + 800/800)/2 = (0.25 + 1.0)/2 = 0.625$. Response 2 needed all its tokens, so it counts as fully efficient even though it is long.

lessons.title: Why RL makes reasoning long: the length bias in the policy loss

blocks.md:
Fatemi et al. (2025) ran PPO on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with just 4 OlympiadBench (olympiad-level math and physics) problems that the model never solved, however often it was sampled. Every response got the same reward, -0.5. Accuracy stayed at zero, yet response length kept climbing while the policy loss fell. The model was not learning to think harder about problems it could not solve; the optimizer was finding that longer failures cost less.

This lesson explains why, because it decides the fix. If RL lengthens traces through the loss, the remedy is in the loss, not a length penalty stacked on top.

The GRPO side you already know from the grpo-rlvr course (lesson 7): GRPO divides each response's token sum by its length $|o_i|$, so each token of a wrong 1,000-token answer is pushed down 10 times less than each token of a wrong 100-token answer. Liu et al. (2025), who propose **Dr. GRPO**, saw GRPO keep lengthening responses after reward gains slowed; removing the $1/|o_i|$ and std terms stopped the runaway growth and substantially shortened incorrect responses. They also found the same per-response or per-batch length normalization in the PPO losses of trl, OpenRLHF, verl and other open-source code, and replaced it with a constant such as the generation budget.

PPO adds a second route. It estimates each token's advantage with **generalized advantage estimation** (GAE): a sum of future **temporal-difference errors** $\delta_t = r_t + V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)$, the surprise in the value estimate $V$ at each step, each weighted by $\lambda$ raised to its distance. With $\gamma = 1$ and a reward only on the last token, token $t$ of a $T$-token response gets roughly $\lambda^{T-1-t}$ times the final surprise $R$, and the loss averages over all $T$ tokens. Fatemi et al. prove that for $\lambda < 1$ the average is about $R / (T(1-\lambda))$.

blocks.caption: Fatemi et al., Theorem 1 (leading term). $R$ is the final reward minus the value predicted before it, $\epsilon$ bounds the per-step value surprises. If $R < 0$ the loss is positive and falls like $1/T$, so longer failed responses lower it; if $R > 0$ shorter ones lower it more.

blocks.code:
def gae(T, r, lam=0.95, values=None):
    """GAE with gamma = 1 and a reward r only on the last token."""
    V = values or [0.0] * T                # value estimates V(s_t)
    adv, run = [0.0] * T, 0.0
    for t in reversed(range(T)):
        nxt = V[t + 1] if t + 1 < T else 0.0
        delta = (r if t == T - 1 else 0.0) + nxt - V[t]
        run = delta + lam * run
        adv[t] = run
    return adv

for r in (-0.5, 1.0):
    for T in (100, 1000, 10000):
        A = gae(T, r)
        loss = -sum(A) / T      # PPO loss with ratio 1, averaged over T
        print(f"r={r:+.1f} T={T:>5}: first-token A={A[0]:+.2e}  loss={loss:+.5f}")
blocks.caption: Runs as shown. Real output: for r = -0.5 the loss is +0.09941 at T = 100, +0.01000 at 1,000 and +0.00100 at 10,000; for r = +1 it is -0.19882, -0.02000 and -0.00200. The first token's advantage vanishes (about 1e-23 at T = 1,000) because lambda^999 is tiny.

blocks.title: PPO loss of one response vs its length (GAE, gamma = 1)

scenes.caption: Simplified: value estimates 0, importance ratio 1. A failed answer (reward -0.5, the PPO penalty Fatemi et al. used) has a positive loss that shrinks like 1/T: 0.099 at 100 tokens, 0.010 at 1,000.
A correct answer (reward +1) has a negative loss whose size also shrinks like 1/T, so being short lowers it most. The sign of the reward decides which way length is pulled.
Raise lambda toward 1 and the curves flatten at short lengths: the advantage decays more slowly along the response, so more tokens share the terminal reward before the 1/T dilution takes over.

blocks.prompt: What if you set lambda = 1, so the terminal reward reaches every token undiluted? Does a failed response still lower its loss by growing?
blocks.reveal: **No, but you trade one problem for another.** With $\lambda = 1$ the leading term becomes $-R$, independent of $T$, so the $1/T$ pull disappears. The error term, however, now grows linearly with $T$: value-estimation noise on long responses swamps the signal, and Fatemi et al. report slower or unstable training. Their recommendation is $\lambda < 1$ (they used 0.95) plus problems the model can sometimes solve.

blocks.md: GRPO behaves differently on unsolvable problems: when all $G$ answers in a group are wrong every advantage is 0, so those groups add no length pressure (and no learning). The pressure comes from wrong answers in **mixed** groups, whose advantage is negative; Fatemi et al. show that lowering the probability of the final token then reduces the loss, which favors longer responses. Groups that are all wrong leave only the KL term: their GRPO run on 4 unsolvable problems collapsed to responses under 80 tokens. Dead groups are covered in grpo-rlvr lesson 7.

The two papers do not agree on the exact mechanism. Fatemi et al. argue that the $1/|o_i|$ account is incomplete, because a longer response also adds more terms to the sum being divided. They agree on the direction that matters in practice: negative advantages pull toward longer responses, positive ones toward shorter. The share of wrong answers in training therefore steers length.

blocks.title: Mean length of correct vs incorrect answers (Fatemi et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. Incorrect answers average 3.3 times the length of correct ones on MATH500 (11,519 vs 3,518) and 1.9 times on AIME24 (14,269 vs 7,462).
DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B shows the same gap: 3,204 vs 10,436 on MATH500 and 6,953 vs 14,576 on AIME24. This split, tracked during training, is the diagnostic.

blocks.md:
So track **two** length curves during RL, one for correct rollouts and one for incorrect ones. If incorrect length climbs while correct length stays flat and reward has stalled, suspect the loss before crediting deeper thinking. Read the gap with care: Liu et al. suggest that harder questions need longer answers and are also more often wrong, so part of any gap is difficulty.

The bias can also shorten. Arora and Zanette, using a length-normalized RLOO implementation (RLOO: a leave-one-out baseline instead of the group mean), saw responses shrink even with their length penalty switched off. With the normalization removed, length did not change.

Fatemi et al. turn the analysis into a recipe, **two-phase RL**. Phase 1 trains on hard problems for capability and accepts that length grows, since most answers are wrong. Phase 2 is short: PPO on a handful of problems the model solves only sometimes (success probability above 0), where positive rewards appear and the same loss dynamics now favor short answers. They used just 8 problems from the MATH training set for phase 2 on R1-Distill-Qwen 1.5B and 7B.

blocks.title: Second RL phase on 8 MATH problems, R1-Distill-1.5B (Fatemi et al.)

scenes.caption: Mean response tokens before and after the short PPO phase: 4,842 to 1,965, 12,104 to 6,752, 7,847 to 2,936 and 2,597 to 821. Averaged over the four sets, 54% shorter.

Accuracy (%) for the same runs: 84.2 to 81.0, 32.5 to 30.0, 70.6 to 69.4 on math, and 40.6 to 53.1 on MMLU-STEM (multiple-choice science and engineering). Math accuracy dips 1.2 to 3.2 points; the out-of-domain set rises.

blocks.md: Response length growth during RL is partly an optimizer artifact. Check the loss normalization (a constant normalizer as in Dr. GRPO, $\lambda < 1$ for PPO) and the mix of solvable problems before adding a length penalty, and log length separately for correct and incorrect rollouts.

blocks.question: During a GRPO run, reward has been flat for 200 steps while mean response length keeps rising. Split by outcome, correct responses hold at about 1,500 tokens and incorrect ones grow from 3,000 to 7,000. What should you change first?
options: Add a large constant penalty per token so every response shrinks
Lower the temperature so the model explores less
Train longer: length growth means the model is learning to think more deeply
Replace per-response length normalization in the loss with a constant normalizer (Dr. GRPO), then re-check the two length curves
blocks.explain: Growth confined to wrong answers with no reward gain is the signature of the loss bias: wrong answers are penalized less per token as they lengthen. Fix the normalizer first. A blanket length penalty would also shorten the correct answers, which are not the problem.

blocks.question: PPO with gamma = 1, lambda = 0.95 and value estimates near 0 sees a failed response (reward -0.5). Its per-token-averaged loss is about 0.099 at 100 tokens. About what is it at 1,000 tokens, and which way does that pull length?
options: About 0.010: the loss falls like 1/T, so longer failed responses are favored
About 0.99: the loss grows with T, so shorter responses are favored
About 0.099: GAE makes the loss independent of length
About -0.010: the sign flips once the response is long enough
blocks.explain: The leading term is $-R/(T(1-\lambda)) = 0.5/(T \times 0.05)$: 0.1 at T = 100 and 0.01 at T = 1,000 (exactly 0.0994 and 0.0100 in the code). A smaller loss for a longer failure is the pull toward length.

lessons.title: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO

blocks.md: Lesson 2 compressed traces offline. RL offers a more direct lever: add a length term to the reward and let the policy discover where it can cut. The Kimi k1.5 report notes that response length grows significantly during RL training; lesson 3 showed that part of such growth can come from the loss itself, and that part is best fixed in the loss. But even with an unbiased loss, a correctness-only reward has no reason to prefer a short correct answer over a long one. Kimi found the growth brought better performance but was costly at training and inference time, and overthinking is often not what users want.

Recall GRPO: for one prompt the policy samples a group of $k$ responses, each gets a scalar reward, and each response's advantage is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation. With a 0/1 correctness reward, every correct response in a group gets the **same** advantage, however long it is.

Kimi k1.5 adds a **length reward** computed within each group of $k$ sampled responses. Kimi does not train with GRPO itself. Its update is a variant of **online mirror descent**: at each iteration the current model becomes the reference, and the new policy maximizes expected reward minus $\tau$ times its KL divergence from that reference, so every step stays close to the previous policy. The exact solution needs a normalizer that Kimi approximates with the **mean reward** of the $k$ samples, so the update is a policy gradient with the group mean as baseline, no division by the standard deviation. GRPO uses the same mean baseline and only rescales by the std, so plugging the same reward into GRPO below keeps the ordering of advantages. With $\text{len}(i)$ the length of response $i$ and min_len, max_len the extremes in the group:

blocks.caption: In words: $\lambda_i$ is 0.5 minus where response $i$ sits between the shortest and longest length in its group, as a fraction of that range: +0.5 (shortest) to -0.5 (longest). Wrong answers get at most 0, so brevity never pays when wrong. If all lengths are equal the term is 0.

blocks.title: One GRPO group with the Kimi k1.5 length reward

scenes.caption: Correctness reward only. A, B and C all get 1 and the same advantage (+0.816): GRPO reinforces the 1900-token answer exactly as much as the 300-token one.
Length reward. min_len = 300, max_len = 1900, so lambda = 0.5 - (len - 300) / 1600: 0.5, 0.25, -0.5 for the right ones. Wrong D gets min(0, 0.375) = 0, wrong E gets -0.25.
Total reward with an illustrative weight 0.5 on the length term: 1.25, 1.125, 0.75, 0, -0.125.

Group-normalized advantages (dividing by the population standard deviation, over k rather than k - 1): +1.147, +0.926, +0.265, -1.059, -1.279. The long correct answer is still reinforced, but far less than the short one.

blocks.md: Two details from the report matter in practice. The length reward is added to the correctness reward with a weighting parameter (its value is not given). And it slowed training early on, so they **warm it up**: standard RL first, then a constant length penalty for the rest of training. For their long2short RL phase they also sharply reduced the maximum rollout length. The resulting short model scored 60.8 Pass@1 (percent of problems solved by one sampled answer) on AIME 2024 while using 3,272 tokens on average.

DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization, from ByteDance Seed and Tsinghua AIR, 2025) meets length from the other side: the **maximum** length. RL rollouts are truncated at a limit, and the default is to give truncated samples a punitive reward. DAPO argues that this injects **reward noise**: a sound reasoning process can be punished purely for being long. Their first fix, **overlong filtering**, masks truncated samples out of the loss. Their second, **soft overlong punishment**, adds a graded penalty:

blocks.tex: R_{\text{length}}(y) = \begin{cases} 0 & |y| \le L_{\max} - L_{\text{cache}} \\ \dfrac{(L_{\max} - L_{\text{cache}}) - |y|}{L_{\text{cache}}} & L_{\max} - L_{\text{cache}} < |y| \le L_{\max} \\ -1 & |y| > L_{\max} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: $|y|$ is the response length, $L_{\max}$ the hard limit and $L_{\text{cache}}$ the soft zone just below it. The penalty is 0 up to $L_{\max} - L_{\text{cache}}$, falls linearly to -1 at $L_{\max}$, and is -1 beyond. It is added to the rule-based correctness reward.

scenes.caption: DAPO's setting: expected maximum 16,384 tokens plus a 4,096-token soft zone, so generation stops at 20,480. Below 16,384 the penalty is 0.
Inside the soft zone the penalty falls linearly: a correct 18,432-token answer earns 1 - 0.5 = 0.5. At 20,480 and beyond (truncated) it is -1.
Shrink the soft zone to 1,024 tokens and the ramp becomes a near cliff, close to the default of simply punishing truncated samples.

blocks.code:
def length_rewards(lengths, correct, step, w=0.5, warmup=100,
                   l_max=20480, l_cache=4096):
    """One group of completions for one prompt. Returns total rewards."""
    lo, hi = min(lengths), max(lengths)
    out = []
    for n, ok in zip(lengths, correct):
        r = 1.0 if ok else 0.0
        # Kimi k1.5 group-relative length reward, after warm-up
        if step >= warmup and hi > lo:
            lam = 0.5 - (n - lo) / (hi - lo)
            r += w * (lam if ok else min(0.0, lam))
        # DAPO soft overlong punishment
        if n > l_max:
            r += -1.0
        elif n > l_max - l_cache:
            r += ((l_max - l_cache) - n) / l_cache
        out.append(r)
    return out

def grpo_adv(r):
    m = sum(r) / len(r)
    sd = (sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in r) / len(r)) ** 0.5
    return [(x - m) / sd for x in r]

L = [300, 700, 1900, 500, 1500]
C = [True, True, True, False, False]
for step in (50, 500):
    r = length_rewards(L, C, step)
    print(step, [round(x, 3) for x in r],
          [round(a, 3) for a in grpo_adv(r)])
print(length_rewards([18432], [True], 500))
blocks.caption: Both rewards per group, as a GRPO trainer calls them. Output: at step 50 (warm-up) only correctness counts, advantages 0.816 and -1.225; at step 500 rewards 1.25, 1.125, 0.75, 0, -0.125 and advantages 1.147, 0.926, 0.265, -1.059, -1.279, as in the figure. A lone 18,432-token correct answer gets 0.5.

blocks.md: In DAPO's ablation, which adds one component at a time, on AIME 2024 (accuracy averaged over 32 samples per problem, written avg@32; Qwen2.5-32B base), naive GRPO reached 30; adding overlong filtering gave 36; clip-higher, which raises the upper clipping bound on the policy ratio so unlikely tokens can grow, gave 38; soft overlong punishment then gave 41. These are cumulative additions, so each number includes the earlier fixes.

DAPO's soft penalty is a **training stability** tool, not a conciseness objective. It is zero for any length below 16,384 tokens, so it does nothing about a 2,000-token answer to an easy question. Kimi's group-relative reward is the one that pushes toward shorter correct answers at every length.

A third design normalizes length per prompt. Arora and Zanette (CMU, 2025) multiply correctness by a length discount: the reward is $1 - \alpha f$ for a correct response and 0 for a wrong one, where $f$ squashes the response's length, standardized by the mean and standard deviation of the **correct** responses' lengths for that prompt, through a sigmoid $\sigma$. Because $f$ stays between 0 and 1 and $\alpha < 1$, a correct answer, however long, always beats a wrong one. One coefficient $\alpha$ sets how hard the model is pushed; lesson 8 compares the resulting models.

blocks.caption: mean(x) and std(x) are estimated from the correct rollouts for prompt $x$ during training, so a 9,000-token answer to a hard problem is judged against other answers to that problem, not against GSM8K answers.

blocks.md: Arora and Zanette also show why they do **not** divide advantages by the group std. In a group where every response is correct, each reward is $1 - \alpha f_i$, so its deviation from the mean is $-\alpha (f_i - \bar f)$ and the std is $\alpha$ times the std of the $f_i$. Dividing one by the other cancels $\alpha$: the shortest answer gets the same advantage whether $\alpha$ is 0.01 or 0.4 (about $+\sqrt 3$ if the rewards are spread uniformly). The knob stops working, and in their runs normalized advantages cut length quickly but took accuracy down with it. The same cancellation hits the Kimi weight in this lesson's GRPO example whenever a group is all correct; Kimi's own update uses the mean-only baseline, which keeps the weight meaningful.

Group-relative length rewards are scale-free: a 300 vs 1,900 token group and a 3,000 vs 19,000 token group get the same +0.5 to -0.5 spread. That keeps the term meaningful on both easy and hard prompts, where absolute lengths differ by 10x.
A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

blocks.question: In a GRPO group, all 8 sampled responses are correct but their lengths differ. With correctness reward only, what is the policy gradient signal from this group?
options: Zero: every reward is equal, so every advantage is 0, and length gets no push either way
Strongly favors the shortest response
Strongly favors the longest response
Negative for all responses, since the mean is subtracted
blocks.explain: Equal rewards give zero advantages, so the group teaches nothing. Kimi's length reward breaks the tie inside such groups, which is exactly where length can be cut without hurting accuracy.

blocks.question: A team trains with a hard rule 'reward = -1 if truncated at 8K tokens' and sees training become unstable as responses approach 8K. Which change follows the DAPO findings?
options: Raise the penalty to -10 so the model learns faster
Remove the correctness reward for long responses
Mask truncated samples from the loss, or ramp the penalty linearly over a soft zone before the limit
Lower the learning rate only for long responses
blocks.explain: Overlong filtering (masking) and soft overlong punishment both reduce reward noise from punishing reasoning that was merely cut off. A bigger cliff adds more noise, not less.

blocks.question: You train with the Arora-Zanette reward and GRPO's std-normalized advantages. On prompts where all 8 samples are correct, you double alpha from 0.1 to 0.2. What happens to the advantages in those groups?
options: They double, so the push toward short answers doubles
Nothing: alpha cancels between the deviation and the std, so the advantages are identical
They halve, because the std grows faster than the deviation
They become zero, because all samples are correct
blocks.explain: Every reward is $1 - \alpha f_i$, so both the deviation from the mean and the std scale with alpha and the ratio does not. Zero would be right for a correctness-only reward; here the length term breaks the tie. To keep alpha meaningful, use the plain deviation (no std), as Arora and Zanette do.

lessons.title: L1: putting the token budget in the prompt

blocks.md: Length penalties make a model shorter on average, but a user still cannot say 'spend about 1,000 tokens on this'. **L1** (Aggarwal and Welleck, CMU, 2025) makes the budget an input. Its training method, **Length Controlled Policy Optimization (LCPO)**, is ordinary GRPO with two changes: the prompt gets a target length, and the reward scores both correctness and how well the length matches.

blocks.title: Asking an untrained reasoning model for a length

scenes.caption: The requested lengths, as 'Think for exactly N tokens.' in the prompt.
What DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview, a 1.5-billion-parameter reasoning model that L1 is trained from (no LCPO), actually generated: 5,491 to 6,421 tokens, regardless of the request (L1 paper, Table 5).

blocks.md: Prompting alone fails, as the bars show. So does supervised fine-tuning on responses relabeled with their own lengths: the SFT model in the paper's appendix still produced 20,903 to 22,749 tokens for every request from 512 to 4,096. The authors' explanation is that without an online, length-sensitive reward the model never learns to adjust its reasoning to a budget.
LCPO appends 'Think for $n_{gold}$ tokens.' to each training prompt, where the target length $n_{gold}$ is drawn uniformly from 100 to 4,000. The **L1-Exact** reward is:

blocks.tex: r(y, y_{gold}, n_{gold}) = \mathbb{I}(y = y_{gold}) - \alpha \cdot \lvert n_{gold} - n_y \rvert, \qquad \alpha = 0.0003
blocks.caption: The first term is 1 if the answer $y$ matches the reference answer $y_{gold}$, else 0. From it subtract $\alpha$ times the gap between the target $n_{gold}$ and the generated length $n_y$, in either direction. With the paper's $\alpha = 0.0003$, each 1,000 tokens off costs 0.3.

blocks.md: **L1-Max** then fine-tunes L1-Exact for a 'Think for maximum N tokens.' prompt. Its reward multiplies correctness by a soft ramp: $\alpha$ times the tokens left under budget, plus $\delta = 0.5$, clipped to the range 0 to 1. So a correct answer exactly at budget earns 0.5, more if shorter, less if over. The $\delta = 0.5$ term means a correct answer slightly over budget still beats a wrong one, and the ramp keeps a gradient for GRPO where a hard cutoff would give none.

blocks.caption: Max mode is trained on both prompt types: exact-length prompts use the Exact reward, maximum prompts use this one.

blocks.title: LCPO rewards as a function of output length

scenes.caption: L1-Exact with the paper's alpha = 0.0003 and target 1,024. A correct answer peaks at 1 exactly on target; 1,500 tokens gives 0.857, 600 tokens gives 0.873.
The trade: a correct 4,500-token answer (3,476 off target) scores -0.043, below a wrong answer of exactly 1,024 tokens (0). Past 1 / alpha = 3,333 tokens of error, length dominates.

L1-Max: correctness times a clipped ramp, drawn with an illustrative alpha of 0.001 (the paper gives no Max value). At the budget a correct answer earns 0.5; shorter earns more (here 1.0 at 524 tokens); wrong answers earn 0 at any length.
Move the target to 2,048: the whole reward shape slides. One policy learns to read the number in the prompt and aim for it.

blocks.prompt: The authors also tried an additive Max reward: correctness minus a length penalty, instead of correctness times a ramp. It achieved a 0% budget violation rate. Why did they reject it?
blocks.reveal: The model **collapsed to extremely short chains of thought**. Short outputs trivially satisfy any maximum, and with an additive penalty a short wrong answer loses little compared with a long right one. Multiplying by correctness means length can only scale a reward the model already earned; brevity alone earns nothing. Accuracy dropped substantially, so the perfect violation rate was a reward hack.

blocks.md: Results, on a 1.5B model (DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview) trained with 4K context: on math sets the mean length error is close to 3%, and L1-Max misses its budget by more than 500 tokens only 1.3% of the time on average. Against s1 budget forcing (stopping or extending the thinking at decode time, lesson 7) at 512 and 1,024 tokens, L1 is 20 to 25 points higher in absolute terms. Accuracy is roughly linear in log length, with slope 0.24 for L1 vs 0.37 for s1, because L1 loses much less at small budgets.

A side effect: trained long-CoT models become strong **short reasoning models**. At about 816 average tokens, L1-Max averaged 47.8% across AIME, MATH (the full competition set behind MATH500), AMC (the American Mathematics Competitions, a step below AIME) and OlympiadBench (olympiad-level math and physics problems) vs 45.6% for GPT-4o at 840 tokens.

L1-Exact spends the requested budget even when the problem is easy, because its reward penalizes being too short. When the goal is a worst-case cost cap rather than an exact length, use the Max formulation, which matched or beat L1-Exact while often using up to 2x fewer tokens.
Length control needs an online reward that sees the generated length. The prompt carries the budget; the RL reward is what teaches the model to honor it.

blocks.question: With L1-Exact (alpha = 0.0003) and a target of 1,024 tokens, which response gets the highest reward?
options: Wrong answer, exactly 1,024 tokens
Correct answer, 4,500 tokens
Correct answer, 1,500 tokens
Correct answer, 6,000 tokens
blocks.explain: Rewards: 0, -0.043, 0.857 and -0.493. A correct answer close to the target wins; a correct answer more than 3,333 tokens off scores below a wrong one.

blocks.question: Why does the L1-Max reward multiply by correctness instead of adding a length penalty?
options: Multiplication is faster to compute during GRPO
So that brevity is only rewarded on correct answers, which prevents collapse into very short wrong outputs
Because GRPO cannot handle negative rewards
So that responses over budget always get reward 0 regardless of correctness
blocks.explain: The additive variant was ablated and collapsed to very short CoTs. With a product, a wrong answer earns 0 at any length, so shortening only pays when the answer stays correct.

lessons.title: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment

blocks.md:
Overthinking is waste after the answer is already right. The opposite failure wastes tokens too. Wang et al. (Tencent AI Lab, 2025) gave QwQ-32B-Preview an AIME problem about two ellipses. Its first thought, 411 tokens long, set up a valid approach. Then it wrote 'Alternatively', tried a geometric view, then an optimization view, and kept switching: 25 thoughts and 7,681 tokens later it gave a guessed answer.

They call this **underthinking**: switching between reasoning approaches too often to take any of them deep enough. A **thought** here is one stretch of reasoning between such switches, which Llama-3.3-70B located by finding phrases like 'alternatively' that truly start a new approach.

blocks.title: QwQ-32B-Preview on one AIME problem: 25 thoughts, one answer

scenes.caption: Each thought after the first opens with 'Alternatively'. Lengths from the paper's Figure 2: five thoughts, then 20 more averaging 284 tokens. Total 7,681 tokens, ending in a guessed answer.

T1 noticed that both equations describe ellipses and set them equal, a valid route to the answer. Judged by two R1-distilled models, it would have succeeded if carried through. The model left it after 411 tokens.

Every token after the first correct thought did not help: underthinking score 1 - 411 / 7,681 = 0.946. Overthinking wastes tokens after a right answer; underthinking wastes them by abandoning a right approach.

blocks.md: The pattern is systematic. On AIME 2024, o1-like models used on average 225% more tokens in incorrect responses than in correct ones, with 418% more thought switches. Switching grows with difficulty across MATH500 levels. And over 70% of incorrect responses contained at least one correct thought, judged by two DeepSeek-R1 distilled models that were themselves checked on 90 labeled AIME thoughts (about 82% accurate). The models often find a right road and leave it.

blocks.caption: Underthinking score over the $N$ incorrect responses: $\hat T_i$ counts tokens up to and including the first correct thought, $T_i$ all tokens. With no correct thought $\hat T_i = T_i$, scoring 0: that is not underthinking but not knowing how to solve it. Lower is better.

blocks.md: Long output does not tell you which failure you have. Overthinking re-solves an easy problem that was already right; underthinking abandons a promising approach on a hard one. The fixes differ: stop earlier in the first case, stay longer on each idea in the second.

The fix Wang et al. propose works at decoding time, with no training. The **thought-switching penalty** (TIP) subtracts a constant $\alpha$ from the logits (the scores before softmax) of switch tokens such as 'alternatively', but only during the first $\beta$ tokens of each thought. Switching stays possible, just less likely before an idea has had room to develop. A grid search on AIME 2022 and 2023 chose $\alpha = 3$ and $\beta = 600$; a strong penalty held for too long hurt accuracy.

blocks.tex: \hat z_{t,v} = \begin{cases} z_{t,v} - \alpha & \text{if } v \in \hat V \text{ and } t < \Psi + \beta \\ z_{t,v} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: $z_{t,v}$ is the logit of token $v$ at position $t$, $\hat V$ the set of switch tokens, $\Psi$ the position where the current thought started. With $\alpha = 0$ or $\beta = 0$ this is ordinary decoding.

blocks.code:
import math

def tip(logits, switch_ids, pos_in_thought, alpha=3.0, beta=600):
    """Thought-switching penalty: lower switch-token logits early in a thought."""
    if pos_in_thought < beta:
        logits = [z - alpha if i in switch_ids else z
                  for i, z in enumerate(logits)]
    return logits

def softmax(z):
    m = max(z)
    e = [math.exp(x - m) for x in z]
    s = sum(e)
    return [x / s for x in e]

vocab = ["Alternatively", "So", "Let", "Therefore"]
z = [2.0, 1.5, 1.0, 0.5]            # toy logits at one position
for pos in (120, 700):
    p = softmax(tip(z, {0}, pos))
    print(pos, {w: round(q, 3) for w, q in zip(vocab, p)})
print("no penalty", {w: round(q, 3) for w, q in zip(vocab, softmax(z))})
blocks.caption: Runs as shown. Real output: 120 tokens into a thought, 'Alternatively' falls from 0.455 to 0.04 and the other tokens absorb the mass; at 700 tokens (past beta) the distribution is untouched. In a real decoder this is a logits processor applied at every step.

blocks.title: Thought-switching penalty on AIME 2024 (Wang et al., Table 3)

scenes.caption: Pass@1 (%) from 32 samples per problem. TIP raises QwQ from 38.3 to 44.1, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B from 61.4 to 64.1 and DeepSeek-R1 from 73.8 to 74.8. A prompt asking R1 to finish each idea gave 72.4.
Thought-switching tokens per response fall: 16.1 to 13.9, 8.2 to 4.5, and 13.8 to 5.7 for R1 (12.0 with the prompt). The gap between switches grows, for R1 from 580 to 942 tokens.

blocks.md: Early exit attacks the overthinking side without training. **DEER** (Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning, Yang et al., 2025) starts from a measurement: forcing the model to answer at different points of its thinking showed that about 75% of samples contain a point where stopping already gives the right answer. DEER watches for transition words such as 'Wait', makes the model write a trial answer there, and scores it by the **geometric mean** of each answer token's top probability. Above a threshold $\lambda = 0.95$ it ends the thinking; below it, it discards the trial and lets the model continue.

blocks.title: DEER: try an answer at each pause, exit when confident (simplified)

scenes.caption: Decode as usual until a transition point. DEER uses words such as 'Wait' that mark a switch between reasoning actions (an entropy test also works).

At the first 'Wait', append an answer inducer (a prompt that opens the final answer, e.g. a boxed-answer prefix) and generate a trial answer. Illustrative numbers: trial '12' with token probabilities 0.62 and 0.91.
0.751 is below 0.95, so the trial is thrown away and thinking resumes exactly where it paused.
Second pause: a 10-token answer, nine tokens at 0.999 and one at 0.60. Geometric mean 0.949, so DEER continues. An arithmetic mean (0.959) would have exited: one shaky token is easy to average away.
Third pause: the same answer with the weak token now at 0.97. Confidence 0.996 exceeds 0.95: close the thinking and write the final answer from the trace so far.

blocks.caption: The exit rule with the trace's illustrative numbers. Real output: 0.751 (no exit), 0.949 geometric vs 0.959 arithmetic (only the arithmetic mean would exit), 0.996 (exit). DEER's paper found the arithmetic mean caused more wrong early exits.

blocks.title: DEER on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (Yang et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: Mean generated tokens: 1,484 to 917, 3,858 to 2,143 and 13,765 to 9,839. The cut is largest in relative terms on the easier sets.

Accuracy (%) rises at the same time: 89.6 to 90.6, 87.4 to 89.8 and 41.7 to 49.2 (AIME24 averaged over 4 samples per problem). Stopping earlier avoids some reasoning that talks itself out of a right answer.

blocks.md:
Across 11 models and 10 benchmarks DEER shortened reasoning by 19.1% to 80.1% on average while accuracy rose 0.3 to 5.0 points, with the same 0.95 threshold everywhere. Model confidence turned out polarized, mostly above 0.97 or below 0.9, which is why the threshold is not fragile. Each trial answer costs extra decoding; a branch-parallel variant of DEER overlaps it with continued reasoning.

**DeepConf** (Fu et al., 2025) applies confidence to parallel sampling: it averages a token confidence (the negative mean log probability of the top-$k$ candidates) over sliding windows of e.g. 2,048 tokens and stops any trace whose window confidence falls below a threshold set from 16 warm-up traces. It cut generated tokens by up to 84.7% against full parallel thinking on AIME 2025. Voting over the survivors is covered in test-time-compute-scaling.

**TokenSkip** (Xia et al., 2025) is the offline counterpart: compress the trace itself. It scores each CoT token's importance with LLMLingua-2, a small bidirectional token classifier trained to label which tokens to keep (the semantic-caching-prompt-compression course, not a prerequisite, covers it in depth), keeps the most important fraction $\gamma$ (drawn from 0.5 to 1.0) of each correct training trace, writes $\gamma$ into the prompt and fine-tunes with LoRA. On Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct it cut GSM8K reasoning from 313 to 181 tokens (40%) with under 0.4 points of accuracy lost. Those are short instruct-model CoTs; it was not shown on long thinking traces.

Waste has two shapes: thinking past a settled answer (stop it with a confidence test such as DEER) and abandoning good ideas too fast (slow the switching with TIP). Both are cheap decode-time controls that need no retraining, sitting between the RL methods and an API's blunt output cap.

blocks.question: DEER is about to decide at a 'Wait'. The trial answer has four tokens with top probabilities 0.995, 0.995, 0.995 and 0.82, and the threshold is 0.95. What does DEER do?
options: Exit: the arithmetic mean is 0.951, above 0.95
Continue: the geometric mean is 0.948, below 0.95
Exit: three of four tokens exceed 0.95
Continue: any token below 0.9 always blocks an exit
blocks.explain: DEER uses the geometric mean: $(0.995^3 \times 0.82)^{1/4} = 0.948$. The arithmetic mean, 0.951, would exit; it lets one uncertain token hide behind confident ones, which the paper found led to premature wrong exits. There is no per-token veto rule.

blocks.question: A model's wrong AIME answers look like this: a sound approach in the first 400 tokens, then 15 'Alternatively' switches and 8,000 tokens with no conclusion. Which training-free change targets this failure directly?
options: DEER early exit at threshold 0.95
A smaller max_output_tokens cap
A thought-switching penalty on 'Alternatively' during the first few hundred tokens of each thought
Self-consistency over 4 samples of the same model
blocks.explain: This is underthinking: the first idea was right but abandoned. TIP makes the model develop each idea longer before switching. DEER helps when a confident answer already exists; a cap just truncates; voting can help but does not change how each trace reasons.

lessons.title: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference

blocks.md: Lessons 2 to 5 needed training, and lesson 6 added confidence and switching rules at decode time. The bluntest decode-time control is **s1** budget forcing, which the prerequisite course test-time-compute-scaling teaches in lesson 7: to cap thinking, append the end-of-thinking delimiter (with 'Final Answer:') so the model must answer now; to extend it, suppress the delimiter and append 'Wait'. Three of its findings matter for length control. Budget forcing hits the budget 100% of the time by construction, while writing a token budget in the prompt stayed inside it only 40% of the time (the model cannot count its tokens) and a step budget 60% (it wrote fewer, longer steps). Extending saturates and can loop. And sampling until a trace happens to fit a length limit shows inverse scaling, because short samples tend to be the ones that were on the right track.

blocks.question: A model has no length training and you must keep its thinking under 1,000 tokens on every request. Which method guarantees that, and what does the guarantee cost?
options: Put 'think for at most 1,000 tokens' in the prompt; it costs nothing
Ask for at most 5 reasoning steps; steps are easier for the model to count than tokens
Budget forcing: force the end-of-thinking delimiter at 1,000 tokens. Control is exact, but the model may be cut mid-step and answer from an unfinished trace
Sample until a trace fits under 1,000 tokens; accuracy improves as the limit tightens
blocks.explain: s1 measured 100% control for budget forcing, 40% for token-count prompts and 60% for step prompts, which the model gamed with longer steps. Filtering samples by length is not a neutral choice of compute. The price of forcing is accuracy at small budgets, which is why L1's trained budgets beat it there (lesson 5).

blocks.md:
Hosted APIs now expose length control as a product feature, and the official docs describe these controls (exact values and defaults vary by model):

- **OpenAI**: `reasoning.effort` with model-dependent levels such as low, medium and high. Lower effort favors speed and fewer tokens. Reasoning tokens are hidden but billed as output tokens and count toward `max_output_tokens`.
- **Anthropic**: manual extended thinking, now deprecated (Claude 4.7 and later models reject it with an error), takes `budget_tokens` (at least 1,024 and below `max_tokens`), described as a target, not a strict cap. Newer models use adaptive thinking, where an effort setting controls depth and the model may skip thinking on easy inputs at low effort.
- **Google Gemini**: `thinking_level`, with dynamic thinking (the model sets its own thinking depth per request) on by default.

blocks.code:
from openai import OpenAI

MODEL = "your-reasoning-model"   # any model that accepts reasoning.effort
client = OpenAI()
resp = client.responses.create(
    model=MODEL,
    reasoning={"effort": "low"},   # plan a shorter think
    max_output_tokens=6000,         # hard cap on reasoning + answer
    input=[{"role": "user", "content": "Is 391 prime?"}],
)
u = resp.usage
print(resp.status, u.output_tokens,
      u.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens)  # reasoning is billed as output
if (resp.status == "incomplete"
        and resp.incomplete_details.reason == "max_output_tokens"):
    # the cap stopped generation, possibly before any visible text;
    # the reasoning tokens are billed anyway
    print("partial:", resp.output_text or "(no visible output)")
blocks.caption: Not run here (needs an API key and a model name). Fields follow OpenAI's reasoning guide: usage.output_tokens includes output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens, and hitting the cap returns status incomplete, reason max_output_tokens. Effort changes the plan; the cap only stops it.

blocks.md: Worked billing, with the illustrative request in the figure below. At high effort the model thinks for 4,800 tokens and answers in 400: **5,200 output tokens** billed. Add `max_output_tokens=3000` and the call returns incomplete after 3,000 reasoning tokens, all billed, with no answer. A retry at the same effort with a larger cap bills another 5,200, so one answer cost **8,200** output tokens. At low effort the same request thinks for 1,500 and answers in 400: **1,900**. The cap-and-retry path costs 8,200 / 1,900 = 4.3 times as much. OpenAI's guide recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and output when you start, then tuning down from the usage numbers you observe.

blocks.title: Hard output cap vs an effort setting (illustrative request)

scenes.caption: Illustrative numbers. At high effort this request would think for 4,800 tokens and answer in 400.
Same effort with an output cap of 3,000 tokens. The cap does not change how the model plans to think, so generation stops mid-thought: status incomplete, no answer, thinking tokens still billed.
Lower effort instead: the model plans a shorter think and still finishes its answer, here in 1,900 tokens total. Gemini's docs recommend exactly this for cost and latency.

blocks.md: A hard output limit is the API version of s1's maximum, but without the forced 'Final Answer:'. OpenAI's docs say that hitting `max_output_tokens` returns status incomplete, possibly before any visible output. Gemini's docs say the limit is a hard cutoff that does not change how the model allocates thinking, and recommend lowering `thinking_level` rather than setting a small output limit.

The 'Stop Overthinking' survey (Sui et al., Rice University and University of Houston, 2025) organizes the field into three families that map onto this course: **model-based** (RL with length rewards, SFT on variable-length CoT: lessons 2 to 5, plus TokenSkip in lesson 6), **reasoning-output-based** (compressing steps into latent vectors that are never written out as tokens, covered in the latent-reasoning-coconut course, which is not a prerequisite, and stopping dynamically during decoding: lesson 6), and **input-prompt-based** (prompting for brevity, as in Chain of Draft, which asks for terse drafts of each step and matched chain-of-thought accuracy with as little as 7.6% of the tokens, routing easy questions to cheaper reasoning: the effort knob above and lesson 8).

A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

Inference-time levers are cheap but blunt: forcing a stop interrupts reasoning, forcing 'Wait' saturates. Training-time methods (preference pairs, length rewards, LCPO) teach the model to plan a shorter trace, which is why L1 beats budget forcing at small budgets.

blocks.question: A product needs answers under 1,500 output tokens from a reasoning model. Responses often come back incomplete with no visible text. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The model is refusing; rephrase the prompt
The output cap is cutting off hidden reasoning; lower the effort level (or thinking budget) and leave headroom in the cap
Temperature is too high; set it to 0
The cap counts only visible tokens, so raise it to the context length
blocks.explain: Reasoning tokens count toward the output limit. If the model plans a long think, a tight cap truncates it before the answer. Lowering effort changes the plan; the cap only stops it.

blocks.question: A request needs 4,800 reasoning tokens and a 400-token answer at its effort level. With max_output_tokens = 3,000 it fails; you retry at the same effort with the cap raised to 6,000. How many output tokens are billed in total for the two calls?
blocks.explain: The failed call bills its 3,000 reasoning tokens and returns no answer. The retry generates 4,800 + 400 = 5,200, all billed as output. Total 8,200. Lowering effort, not tightening the cap, is how you pay for fewer thinking tokens.

lessons.title: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing

blocks.md:
Every method so far shortens a thinking trace that is assumed to exist. Ma et al. (2025) asked whether it needs to exist. Their **NoThinking** prompt prefills the reasoning model's thinking box with one line, 'Okay, I think I have finished thinking.', then the end-of-thinking delimiter, so the model writes its final solution directly. For lesson 1's 2 + 3, that is the difference between 901 tokens and a handful.

On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, NoThinking used 2.0 to 5.1 times fewer tokens. It trailed Thinking on most math and coding sets at one sample, but caught up as more samples were allowed, and matched Thinking on formal theorem proving at 3.3 to 3.7 times fewer tokens.

blocks.title: Thinking, NoThinking and a learned choice between them

scenes.caption: Default Thinking: the reasoning model writes its long chain of thought inside the thinking box, then a final solution.
NoThinking: the box is prefilled ('Okay, I think I have finished thinking.' then the closing delimiter, or just the delimiter), so the model goes straight to the solution.
Hybrid models such as Qwen3 let the user pick: a /no_think flag or an empty thinking block in the chat template selects the bottom path.
AdaptThink trains the model to pick for itself: the first generated token is either the closing delimiter (skip) or a thinking opener such as 'Alright', chosen per question.

blocks.md: The fair comparison holds tokens fixed. With budget forcing applied to both (lesson 7), NoThinking won at low budgets, for instance 51.3 vs 28.9 on AMC 2023 at 700 tokens. Around 3,500 tokens Thinking was better at one sample, while NoThinking still led once two or more samples were drawn. Under a tight budget, a long trace cut off halfway is worth less than a short answer written in full.

blocks.prompt: For formal theorem proving a checker can verify any proof. You have a fixed latency budget. Is it better to spend it on one long Thinking trace or on many NoThinking samples in parallel, keeping any that verifies?
blocks.reveal: **Parallel NoThinking.** With a perfect verifier, Ma et al. found NoThinking samples beat Thinking (with and without parallel sampling) at 7 times lower latency and even 4 times fewer total tokens. Without a verifier they picked among samples with simple confidence-based selection and still did well on some sets: on OlympiadBench math it beat Thinking with 9 times lower latency. Parallel samples finish together; one long trace is sequential. Selection methods are covered in test-time-compute-scaling.

blocks.md: Hybrid models build both modes into one set of weights. **Qwen3** was trained with a thinking-mode-fusion stage: supervised examples with a `/think` or `/no_think` flag in the user turn, where non-thinking answers keep an empty thinking block. In the Hugging Face chat template, `enable_thinking=False` inserts that empty block. A **thinking budget** came for free: when thinking reaches a user-set length, decoding is halted and the text 'Considering the limited time by the user, I have to give the solution based on the thinking directly now.' is inserted with the closing delimiter, and the model answers from what it has. The report says this was not explicitly trained; it emerged from the fusion.

The modes are far apart on hard problems. Qwen3-235B-A22B scored 85.7 on AIME 2024 thinking and 40.1 without. Fusion also had a price: for Qwen3-32B, thinking-mode AIME 2024 fell from 83.8 to 81.4 after the fusion and general-RL stages. A user-chosen switch is only as good as the user's guess about difficulty.

**AdaptThink** (Zhang et al., 2025) lets the model choose. A pilot on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B with a 16K budget found NoThinking about as accurate as Thinking on MATH500 levels 1 to 3, slightly better on level 1, at far fewer tokens. So the goal is: maximize the chance of skipping thought, subject to accuracy staying at least the original model's. Turning the constraint into a penalty and rescaling gives a simple advantage for a policy-gradient update with PPO-style clipping and no KL term.

blocks.caption: $R$ is 1 for a correct answer, $\bar R_{\text{ref}}(x)$ the original model's accuracy on question $x$ (pre-sampled), and the indicator is 1 when the first token closes the thinking box. $\delta$ is a small bonus for skipping.

blocks.md: Two details make it work. **Cold start**: the original model never starts with the closing delimiter, so on-policy samples contain no NoThinking examples to learn from. AdaptThink draws the first token from a fixed distribution instead, half the closing delimiter and half a thinking opener such as 'Alright', then lets the policy continue, and corrects with the importance ratio. **When skipping wins**: NoThinking is reinforced only if its accuracy plus $\delta$ beats both Thinking's and the reference's. Easy question: Thinking 0.95, NoThinking 0.92, reference 0.94 gives advantages 0.01 and 0.05 + 0.92 - 0.94 = 0.03, so skip. Hard: 0.40, 0.10, 0.38 gives 0.02 vs -0.23, so think.

blocks.title: AdaptThink on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (Zhang et al., Table 1)

scenes.caption: Mean tokens of the original model, always thinking: 978, 4,887 and 12,073.
After AdaptThink: 480, 1,782 and 6,679 tokens, a 53% cut on average.
Share of answers written without thinking (%): 86.9 on GSM8K, 76.8 on MATH500, 40.4 on AIME. The harder the set, the more often the model chooses to think.
Accuracy (%) after training: 83.1, 82.0 and 31.0, up from 79.0, 80.6 and 29.4. Skipping thought on easy questions did not cost accuracy here.

blocks.md:
Arora and Zanette's reward (lesson 4) gives a **family** of models instead of a switch: train once per $\alpha$ in 0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4. For their 7B model, $\alpha = 0.1$ cut MATH reasoning by 36% (about 4,000 to 2,600 tokens) for a 2.2% accuracy loss, and the same $\alpha$ saves far more on easy sets: at 0.2, 83% on GSM8K against 27% on AIME 2024.

To compare any of these, plot accuracy against mean tokens, per difficulty level. A method is **dominated** if another is at least as accurate with no more tokens and better on one of the two; the undominated ones form the **Pareto frontier**. Then ask whether the accuracy gaps exceed the noise: one run on $n$ problems has a 95% interval of about $\pm 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$.

In the figure, DAST (SimPO on pairs ranked by a length-based reward) and O1-Pruner (off-policy RL-style fine-tuning toward shorter traces under an accuracy constraint) are further length-aware fine-tuning methods; Merging averages weights with a non-reasoning model; RFT-mix fine-tunes on correct samples from whichever mode solves each problem more often.

blocks.title: Accuracy vs tokens on MATH500, ten methods on one 1.5B model

scenes.caption: Each point is one method from the AdaptThink paper, all starting from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and evaluated with the same setup. Up and left is better.

Frontier: NoThinking (658), AdaptThink (1,782), DAST (2,428) and Arora-Zanette (3,007). Every other point has a rival at least as accurate with fewer tokens. OverThink, lesson 2's recipe, is dominated by AdaptThink.
A rough 95% interval for one run on 500 problems is about 3.5 points. Most methods sit inside the baseline's band: their accuracy differences are noise, their token differences are not.

On AIME's 30 problems one problem is 3.3 points, and at 30% accuracy the 95% interval is about plus or minus 16 points (a band about 33 wide, far past this slider), so judge efficiency methods on hard sets with many samples per problem.

blocks.code:
# MATH500, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B (AdaptThink paper, Table 1)
runs = {  # name: (accuracy %, mean tokens)
    "Thinking": (80.6, 4887), "NoThinking": (67.2, 658),
    "DPO-shortest": (82.4, 3708), "OverThink": (81.2, 4131),
    "DAST": (83.0, 2428), "O1-Pruner": (82.2, 3212),
    "Arora-Zanette": (85.0, 3007), "ModelMerging": (63.0, 2723),
    "RFT-mix": (72.4, 4341), "AdaptThink": (82.0, 1782),
}

def dominated(a, b):  # b at least as good on both, better on one
    return (b[0] >= a[0] and b[1] <= a[1]) and b != a

frontier = [n for n, v in runs.items()
            if not any(dominated(v, w) for w in runs.values())]
print("frontier:", sorted(frontier, key=lambda n: runs[n][1]))

n = 500                                 # problems in MATH500
for acc in (80.6, 85.0):
    p = acc / 100
    half = 1.96 * (p * (1 - p) / n) ** 0.5 * 100
    print(f"{acc}%: 95% CI +/- {half:.1f} points")
blocks.caption: Runs as shown. Real output: frontier NoThinking, AdaptThink, DAST, Arora-Zanette (in token order); the 95% half-width is 3.5 points at 80.6% and 3.1 at 85.0% for 500 problems. Two runs on the same problems compare more tightly with a paired test, but the order of magnitude holds.

blocks.md: Deciding whether to think is often a bigger lever than shortening the thinking. Evaluate every option, from NoThinking to full thinking, on an accuracy-versus-tokens frontier per difficulty level, and check whether accuracy differences exceed the noise of your test set.

blocks.question: Same paper, 7B model, MATH500 (accuracy %, mean tokens): Thinking 90.2 at 3,674; NoThinking 80.6 at 697; DPO-shortest 91.6 at 2,499; Arora-Zanette 91.8 at 2,899; AdaptThink 92.0 at 1,875. Which configurations form the Pareto frontier?
options: Thinking and AdaptThink
Arora-Zanette and DPO-shortest
All five: each is best at something
NoThinking and AdaptThink
blocks.explain: AdaptThink is the most accurate and cheaper than everything except NoThinking, so it dominates Thinking, DPO-shortest and Arora-Zanette. NoThinking is the only cheaper point. Note that 92.0 vs 91.8 is well inside the noise on 500 problems: the frontier claim rests on tokens, not on that accuracy gap.

blocks.question: Under AdaptThink with delta = 0.05, a question has Thinking accuracy 0.70, NoThinking 0.62 and reference accuracy 0.68. Which mode does training push toward on this question?
options: Thinking: its average advantage is 0.02, NoThinking's is 0.05 + 0.62 - 0.68 = -0.01
NoThinking: the delta bonus always favors skipping
Neither: the advantages cancel
NoThinking: its accuracy is within 0.1 of Thinking's
blocks.explain: NoThinking would need $0.62 + \delta$ to beat both 0.70 and 0.68, so $\delta$ above 0.08. At 0.05 the question counts as hard enough to think. Raising $\delta$ trades accuracy for tokens; the paper's Table 2 shows the NoThinking share rising with $\delta$.
